passages.text:
Source material for cognitive extraction pipeline. Structured as chronological passages for chunking.

---

Napoleone di Buonaparte was born on 15 August 1769 in Ajaccio, Corsica, barely a year after the island was ceded by Genoa to France. His father, Carlo Buonaparte, was a minor Corsican nobleman who had fought alongside Pasquale Paoli for Corsican independence — and then, when the cause was lost, pragmatically switched his allegiance to France. His mother, Letizia Ramolino, was a woman of extraordinary physical endurance and emotional severity. She bore thirteen children, of whom eight survived, and managed the household with a discipline that Napoleon would later describe as the foundation of his character. "My mother's firmness," he said, "prevented my ruin."

Letizia did not coddle. She expected obedience and administered punishment with an impartiality that bordered on coldness. She slapped, she withheld, she imposed. Napoleon learned early that love was not unconditional — it was the reward for strength, not a right conferred by birth. This was not cruelty; it was Corsican pragmatism in a household with too many mouths and too little money. But the lesson Napoleon absorbed was specific: affection must be earned through competence and dominance, not expected through sentiment.

Carlo was more indulgent but also more political. He cultivated French connections, obtained a certificate of noble descent, and secured scholarships for his sons at French military academies. Napoleon despised his father's accommodation with the French occupiers even as he benefited from it. The contradiction — resenting the system while exploiting it — was one he never resolved. He revered Paoli, the Corsican patriot his father had abandoned, and fantasised about liberating Corsica himself. At nine years old, he already understood power as something to be seized, not requested.

---

In January 1779, Napoleon and his elder brother Joseph were sent to the Collège d'Autun in mainland France. Napoleon spoke no French — only Corsican Italian. The other boys mocked his accent, his small stature, his poverty, and his foreignness. Joseph adapted. Napoleon did not. He refused to assimilate, refused to soften his Corsican identity, refused to pretend he belonged. He converted his isolation into a fortress of contempt: if they would not accept him, he would surpass them.

At the Royal Military School at Brienne, where he transferred in May 1779, the pattern intensified. He was the smallest boy, the poorest boy, the only Corsican. The aristocratic cadets tormented him for his accent and his threadbare clothes. Napoleon responded not with tears but with a cold, watchful fury. He studied obsessively — mathematics, history, geography — not because he loved learning but because excellence was the only weapon available to him. He devoured Plutarch's Lives, Caesar's commentaries, and histories of Alexander the Great. He did not read for pleasure. He read for strategy: how had great men acquired and held power?

He had almost no friends. The few boys who approached him found a companion who was proud, prickly, and emotionally inaccessible. He formed one close friendship, with a boy named Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne, but even Bourrienne noted that Napoleon kept an interior distance. He was already someone who observed others more than he connected with them — classifying people by their usefulness, their competence, their weakness. When his father died in 1785, Napoleon grieved briefly and privately. He was fifteen. He was now, by his own reckoning, the head of the family. Grief was a luxury he could not afford.

---

Napoleon graduated from the École Militaire in Paris in 1785, forty-second out of fifty-eight students — a mediocre result that he attributed to the examiners' prejudice against Corsicans. He was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the artillery, the least fashionable branch of the army and the one where mathematics mattered more than birth. He was sixteen years old, shorter than most of the men he would command, and burning with an ambition that had no clear object. He knew he was destined for greatness. He did not yet know in what form.

The next eight years were a period of restless frustration. He served in garrison towns, took extended leaves to Corsica, involved himself in Corsican politics, and wrote mediocre novellas and political essays. He read voraciously — Rousseau, Voltaire, Montesquieu, Raynal — and developed a political philosophy that combined Enlightenment rationalism with an instinct for authoritarian control. He believed in meritocracy passionately and in democracy not at all. The Revolution, when it came in 1789, thrilled him: it was the destruction of the aristocratic order that had humiliated him at Brienne, the promise that talent could rise without permission from birth.

But the Revolution also disgusted him. He witnessed the storming of the Tuileries in August 1792 — the mob killing the Swiss Guards, the royal family dragged through jeering crowds — and his reaction was not solidarity with the people but contempt for the King's weakness. "If I had been king," he told Bourrienne, "the rabble would never have entered." He saw the Terror not as justice but as chaos, not as liberty but as the failure of a strong hand to impose order. The Revolution confirmed his deepest conviction: that most people were incapable of governing themselves, and that the world required men of will to shape it.

---

In September 1793, the opportunity arrived. The port of Toulon had rebelled against the Revolutionary government and invited the British fleet to occupy the harbour. The Republican besieging force needed an artillery commander. Through a combination of luck, political connections, and the fact that better-qualified officers had fled or been guillotined, the position went to a twenty-four-year-old Corsican captain named Napoleon Bonaparte.

He was electrifying. He surveyed the defences, identified the key position — a promontory called L'Éguillette that commanded the harbour entrance — and presented a plan so clear and audacious that the senior officers, who had been floundering for weeks, adopted it almost immediately. He placed his batteries with a mathematical precision that reflected his training and a tactical imagination that went beyond it. During the assault, he was in the thick of the fighting — a horse was killed under him, he took a bayonet wound to the thigh — and when the British saw that L'Éguillette was lost, they evacuated the harbour.

Toulon fell. Napoleon was promoted to brigadier general at twenty-four. The victory was intoxicating — not merely because it was his first success but because it confirmed everything he believed about himself. He had seen what others could not see. He had acted while others hesitated. He had been right when the senior officers had been wrong. The taste of being right — of having his judgment validated by the falling of a city — was addictive. It produced in him a feeling he would chase for the rest of his life: the conviction that his vision was superior to other men's, and that the world existed to prove it.

---

In October 1795, Napoleon suppressed a royalist uprising in Paris — the famous "whiff of grapeshot" — and was rewarded with command of the Army of the Interior. He was twenty-six, suddenly powerful, suddenly visible. At a salon, he met Rose de Beauharnais, a thirty-two-year-old widow with two children, debts, a languid sensuality, and connections to the Directory's inner circle. She called herself Joséphine. Napoleon fell in love with an intensity that astonished everyone who knew him.

His letters to her during the Italian campaign are among the most passionate in any language. "I awake filled with you," he wrote. "Your image and the intoxicating memory of last night leave my senses no peace." He was abject, desperate, jealous — a man who commanded armies reduced to begging a woman for a letter. He wrote daily, sometimes twice. She replied infrequently and with obvious indifference. The asymmetry tormented him. He needed her approval in a way that directly contradicted everything he believed about self-sufficiency.

They married on 9 March 1796, two days before Napoleon left for Italy. The marriage certificate falsified both their ages — she became younger, he became older — as though the relationship could only exist in a shared fiction. Napoleon's love was real but also possessive and controlling: he wanted Joséphine not as a partner but as an audience for his greatness, a mirror that would reflect back his importance. When she failed to perform this function — when she didn't write, when she took lovers, when she spent money he didn't have — his pain was genuine but his response was rage, not reflection. He could not understand why someone would not want to be consumed by him.

---

passages.section: 6. The Italian Campaign — Glory and Rivalry (1796–1797)
passages.text:
Napoleon arrived in Italy in March 1796 to take command of an army that was starving, unpaid, and demoralised. The officers despised him — too young, too short, too Corsican. Within weeks, he had transformed them. Not through kindness but through a combination of tactical brilliance, relentless energy, and a gift for inspirational rhetoric that bordered on manipulation. "Soldiers," he told them, "you are hungry and nearly naked. The government owes you much but can give you nothing. I will lead you into the most fertile plains in the world. Rich provinces, great cities will be in your power." It was a promise of loot dressed as liberation, and the army loved him for it.

He destroyed the Austrians and Sardinians in a series of battles — Montenotte, Lodi, Arcole, Rivoli — that became legendary for their speed and audacity. At Lodi, he personally led a charge across a bridge under Austrian fire, and his soldiers began calling him le petit caporal — the Little Corporal — with affection and awe. He was happy in a way that only victory made possible. Each battle confirmed his superiority. Each defeated general was evidence that the world's estimation of talent was finally, belatedly, aligning with his own.

But the Italian campaign also revealed his contempt for authority. The Directory in Paris sent him orders; he ignored them. They sent commissioners to supervise him; he marginalised them. He negotiated treaties without authorisation, reorganised Italian states without permission, and sent back looted art as fait accompli. When the Directory protested, he threatened to resign — knowing they could not replace him. He was gloating, though he would not have used the word: the men in Paris who had given him this army as a consolation prize now depended on him for their survival. The reversal gave him a pleasure that was almost physical.

He also discovered the pleasure of others' failure. When General Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte was sent to Italy and displayed independent ambition, Napoleon froze him out. When Bernadotte won a minor engagement without orders, Napoleon did not congratulate him — he reassigned him. The pattern would repeat throughout his career: subordinates who succeeded too visibly were threats, not allies. He could admire competence in the abstract, but confronted with a rival's actual success, his instinct was suppression, not celebration.

---

In May 1798, Napoleon sailed for Egypt with 38,000 men and a contingent of scholars, scientists, and artists. The expedition was ostensibly strategic — to threaten British India and establish French influence in the eastern Mediterranean — but its deeper motivation was mythic. Napoleon wanted to follow in Alexander's footsteps. He wanted to add "conqueror of the East" to his identity. He took a library of books on Egypt, Islam, and ancient history. He intended not merely to conquer but to understand, to catalogue, to possess intellectually as well as militarily.

The military results were mixed. He defeated the Mamluks at the Battle of the Pyramids but then lost his fleet when Nelson destroyed it at Aboukir Bay, stranding the army in Egypt. The campaign in Syria failed — he could not take Acre. Disease killed more soldiers than combat. Napoleon managed these setbacks with a combination of genuine tactical adaptation and shameless propaganda: the scientific expedition, the Description de l'Égypte, the founding of the Institut d'Égypte — all were real achievements designed to conceal a military stalemate.

It was in Egypt that he learned of Joséphine's affair with Hippolyte Charles. The news devastated him. Officers who witnessed his reaction described a man broken — weeping, raging, threatening divorce, declaring that he would never trust again. "I have a great deal of domestic sorrow," he wrote to his brother Joseph, "for the veil has been entirely removed." His response was not introspection but retaliation: he took a mistress, Pauline Fourès, the wife of a junior officer, with a brazenness that humiliated the husband and established a principle Napoleon would maintain for life — that fidelity was a obligation he imposed on others, not one he accepted for himself. The hurt was real, but what he learned from it was not empathy but armour.

---

Napoleon abandoned his army in Egypt in August 1799 — an act that would have ended any other general's career. He sailed for France in secret, leaving behind 30,000 men who would eventually surrender to the British. His justification was that France needed him more than Egypt did. The Directory was weak, corrupt, and militarily failing. He was certain he could do better. He was also certain that if he waited, someone else would seize the opportunity.

The coup of 18 Brumaire, on 9 November 1799, was nearly a disaster. Napoleon's address to the Council of Five Hundred was incoherent — he stumbled over his words, made vague threats about conspiracies, and was shouted down by angry legislators who called him a tyrant and an outlaw. Some grabbed him by the collar. Soldiers had to rescue him from the chamber. It was his brother Lucien, president of the Council, who saved the day — rallying the grenadiers, clearing the hall, and ramming through the constitutional changes that made Napoleon First Consul.

Napoleon hated the memory of his own incompetence that day. He never acknowledged that Lucien had saved the coup. In his own retelling — and he retold it often — he had been calm, commanding, decisive. The gap between what happened and what he remembered was not dishonesty in any simple sense. It was the operation of a mind that genuinely could not tolerate its own failure. He did not suppress the truth; he replaced it with a version that matched his self-image. This capacity for self-mythologising — for believing his own propaganda — was both his greatest strength and the flaw that would eventually destroy him.

---

As First Consul, Napoleon governed France with an energy that was genuinely revolutionary. He worked eighteen-hour days. He dictated letters at a speed that exhausted his secretaries. He reorganised the tax system, established the Bank of France, built roads and canals, created the lycée system of secondary education, and — most enduringly — codified French law into the Civil Code, which would eventually be adopted or adapted by dozens of nations. "My true glory," he said later, "is not in having won forty battles. Waterloo will wipe out the memory of those victories. What nothing can destroy, what will live forever, is my Civil Code."

He meant it. The Code was an expression of his deepest values: rationality, order, clarity, meritocracy — and patriarchal authority. It guaranteed equality before the law and property rights. It also stripped women of legal autonomy, subordinated wives to husbands, and made divorce difficult for women and easy for men. Napoleon saw no contradiction. Women belonged in the domestic sphere; men in the public one. His own experience — Joséphine's infidelity, Letizia's iron discipline — had taught him that women were either to be controlled or to be feared. The Code reflected both lessons.

He reconciled with the Catholic Church through the Concordat of 1801, not because he was religious — he was at best a deist, at worst a cynic — but because he understood that social control required spiritual legitimacy. "Society cannot exist without inequality of fortunes," he said, "and inequality of fortunes cannot exist without religion." He was sorry for the poverty of the people — genuinely moved by the suffering he saw in the provinces — but his empathy was always channelled through the conviction that he, and only he, knew how to fix it. Sympathy without power was sentimentality. Power without sympathy was tyranny. He believed he had both, and that this combination made him unique in history.

---

On 2 December 1804, in the Cathedral of Notre-Dame, Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of the French. Pope Pius VII had been invited to bless the ceremony, but at the moment of coronation, Napoleon took the crown from the altar and placed it on his own head. The gesture was deliberate: he owed his throne to no one, not even God. Then he crowned Joséphine, who wept. He had almost divorced her the year before — she had not given him an heir — but relented at the last moment. His tenderness toward her at the coronation was genuine, and observers who had seen him humiliate her in private were startled by the gentleness with which he placed the diadem on her head.

Eleven months later, on 2 December 1805, he fought and won the Battle of Austerlitz — the greatest military victory of his career and arguably the most brilliant single battle in the history of warfare. He had lured the combined armies of Austria and Russia into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then struck with his main force at the centre, splitting the allied army in two. The timing was perfect. The deception was perfect. The result was total: 27,000 allied casualties against 9,000 French.

His reaction after Austerlitz was revelatory. He toured the battlefield, looking at the dead and wounded, and reportedly said to his aides: "These are my children." There was compassion in the remark — and also ownership. He was sorry for their suffering, but their suffering was evidence of his achievement. He wrote to Joséphine: "I have beaten the Austro-Russian army commanded by the two emperors. I am a little weary. The battle of Austerlitz is the finest of all I have fought." The tone was that of a man reporting a satisfying day's work. He was happy — not joyfully, but with a deep, settled satisfaction that came from the confirmation of everything he believed about himself. Austerlitz was not just a victory. It was proof.

---

Austerlitz made Napoleon the master of Europe, and mastery corrupted his judgment. He imposed the Continental System — a trade blockade against Britain that required every European nation to close its ports to British goods. The policy was strategically incoherent: it punished France's allies more than it punished Britain, it required military enforcement that stretched French resources, and it rested on the assumption that Napoleon could control the entire European coastline. He believed he could because he believed there was no problem his will could not solve.

He redrew the map of Europe with the casual authority of a man rearranging furniture. He abolished the Holy Roman Empire, created the Confederation of the Rhine, installed his brothers on thrones across the continent — Joseph in Spain, Louis in Holland, Jérôme in Westphalia. When his brothers proved incompetent or disloyal, he berated them with a fury that revealed both his genuine frustration and his inability to accept that other Bonapartes were not replicas of himself. "You are a king," he wrote to Louis, "and you forget that you are a French prince." To Jérôme: "You give up the substance for the shadow. Your conduct disgusts me."

He should have seen the signs of overreach. Spain was unconquerable — the guerrilla war that began in 1808 would bleed France for six years and give the English language the word "guerrilla." Russia was ignoring the Continental System. Austria was rearming. But Napoleon could not distinguish between what he wanted to be true and what was true. He dismissed bad news, punished advisers who delivered it, and surrounded himself with men who told him what he wanted to hear. Talleyrand, his most brilliant diplomat, warned him privately that the Continental System was unsustainable. Napoleon's response was to humiliate Talleyrand publicly, calling him "a silk stocking full of excrement" at a formal reception. He could not accept that someone he considered inferior might see more clearly than he did.

---

On 30 November 1809, Napoleon told Joséphine that their marriage was over. She fainted — or appeared to faint. He carried her to her room himself. Both of them wept. He needed an heir, and she could not give him one. The political logic was unanswerable: without a son, his empire would die with him. But the emotional cost was real, and Napoleon paid it honestly, even if he could not articulate what he was losing.

He was sorry for her. This was genuine, not performed. He settled on her the Château de Malmaison, an income of five million francs a year, and the title of Empress. He continued to write to her, to visit her, to ask after her health. When he married Marie Louise of Austria in April 1810 — a political alliance designed to produce a Habsburg heir — he told Joséphine: "I shall always be your friend." He was telling the truth, as far as he understood friendship.

What he could not see was that his sorrow for Joséphine was also sorrow for the person he had been when he loved her. She was the last connection to the young general who had written frantic letters from Italy, who had been vulnerable enough to be destroyed by her infidelity, who had felt things with an intensity that his later power had made impossible. Joséphine represented the emotional life he had sacrificed for the political one. Divorcing her was not just losing a wife — it was closing a door on a version of himself that had been capable of unguarded feeling. He mourned that loss without understanding it.

Marie Louise gave him a son — Napoleon II, King of Rome — in March 1811. He was ecstatic. He had wanted this child with a desperation that revealed how much of his empire-building was ultimately about legacy, about cheating death through dynasty. But his relationship with Marie Louise was dutiful rather than passionate. She was obedient, loyal, and dull. She gave him what Joséphine could not — an heir — but she could not give him what Joséphine had — the feeling of being matched.

---

In June 1812, Napoleon invaded Russia with the Grande Armée — over 600,000 men, the largest army ever assembled in European history. His strategic objective was to force Tsar Alexander I to re-enter the Continental System. His psychological objective was to prove that no one could defy him. He predicted a quick campaign: one or two decisive battles, a humbled Tsar, a return to Paris before winter. He was fortune-telling, and he was wrong.

The Russians refused to fight. They retreated, burning crops and villages behind them, drawing the French deeper into Russia's vastness. Napoleon advanced, waiting for the decisive battle that never came. Borodino, on 7 September, was a pyrrhic victory — 70,000 casualties on both sides, the bloodiest single day in the Napoleonic Wars — but the Russian army was not destroyed. It retreated again. Napoleon entered Moscow on 14 September and found the city burning. Alexander refused to negotiate. Napoleon waited five weeks, convinced the Tsar would come to terms. He could not accept that his presence in Moscow was not, by itself, sufficient to compel surrender. He was applying the logic of Austerlitz to a situation that was not Austerlitz, and his certainty that the past predicted the future was the precise cognitive error that destroyed him.

---

The retreat began on 19 October 1812. It was one of the great catastrophes in military history. The Grande Armée, already weakened by disease, desertion, and the Battle of Borodino, marched back through a landscape it had already stripped bare, in temperatures that dropped to minus thirty degrees. Horses died by the thousands. Soldiers froze in their sleep. The Cossacks harassed the flanks. At the Berezina River crossing, thousands drowned or were trampled.

Napoleon's behaviour during the retreat revealed the complexity of his character. He was, by turns, brilliant and delusional. He organised the rearguard with genuine tactical skill, maintaining enough cohesion to prevent total disintegration. He walked among the soldiers, shared their cold, and made decisions that saved thousands who would otherwise have died at the river crossings. Officers who were there described a leader who was physically brave and mentally present in a way that inspired loyalty even in catastrophe.

But he also refused to acknowledge the scale of what was happening. He dictated bulletins to Paris that minimised the disaster, blamed the weather, blamed the Russians, blamed everything except his own decision to invade. When he finally abandoned the army in December — riding ahead to Paris in a sleigh — he justified it the same way he had justified abandoning Egypt: France needed him more than the army did. The soldiers he left behind had a different view. Of the 600,000 who had crossed into Russia, fewer than 100,000 returned. Napoleon's reaction to this arithmetic was not guilt but calculation: he needed to raise a new army before the coalition powers exploited his weakness. The dead were a cost, not a moral problem.

And yet, at St Helena, he would weep when he spoke of the retreat. "Those poor fellows," he said. "They suffered so much." He was sorry for them — retrospectively, safely, from the distance of exile. Whether he had been sorry for them while they were freezing is a question his own memoirs cannot answer honestly.

---

Napoleon raised a new army with astonishing speed — 350,000 men by spring 1813 — but they were boys, not veterans. The coalition against him now included Russia, Prussia, Austria, Sweden, and Britain. His marshals were exhausted. Talleyrand was secretly negotiating with the allies. Even his closest advisers urged him to negotiate a peace that would preserve France's natural borders — the Rhine, the Alps, the Pyrenees — and his own throne.

He refused. The allies offered generous terms at Prague in the summer of 1813: France could keep Belgium, the Rhineland, and northern Italy. Napoleon would remain Emperor. It was, by any rational calculation, a favourable outcome. But Napoleon could not accept it because acceptance meant acknowledging limits, and acknowledging limits meant admitting he was not the man he believed himself to be. "They want me to give up everything I've built?" he said. "I cannot. I was not raised to such a throne to accept limitations." The statement was sincere. He genuinely could not see that a smaller empire voluntarily accepted was preferable to a larger empire violently lost.

At the Battle of Leipzig in October 1813 — the "Battle of the Nations" — he was defeated by a coalition army nearly twice the size of his own. It was the decisive battle he had always sought, and this time he was on the wrong side of it. He retreated across the Rhine. Germany was lost. The empire was collapsing.

His mood oscillated between manic energy and dark fatalism. He planned counterattacks, dictated orders, reorganised what remained of his forces — and then, in quiet moments, spoke of destiny in a way that suggested he already knew the end. "Fate wills it," he told his aides. "One can do nothing against fate." This was a man who had spent his entire career believing he could shape fate recognising, for the first time, that fate might shape him. The recognition did not produce wisdom. It produced rage.

---

In April 1814, with allied armies in Paris and his marshals refusing to fight, Napoleon abdicated. The scene at Fontainebleau was a study in controlled disintegration. He signed the document, addressed his Old Guard in a farewell ceremony that reduced hardened soldiers to tears, and kissed the regimental eagle. "I would embrace you all," he told them, "but let me embrace your general." He kissed Marshal Petit on both cheeks. The gesture was theatrical and sincere simultaneously — Napoleon could not have distinguished between the two.

He was exiled to the island of Elba, a tiny Mediterranean territory where he was given sovereignty over 12,000 inhabitants and an annual income from the French government. The humiliation was devastating. He had ruled an empire of 70 million people; now he was a petty prince on an island the size of a Paris arrondissement.

On the night of 12 April, alone in his chambers at Fontainebleau, Napoleon attempted suicide. He swallowed a mixture of opium, belladonna, and hellebore — a poison he had carried since the Russian campaign. The dose was old and had lost its potency. He vomited violently through the night but survived. He told his valet Constant: "God has decided I must continue to suffer." The suicide attempt was the clearest evidence that Napoleon's sense of self was entirely dependent on his power. Without the empire, he was not diminished — he was annihilated. He could not imagine a life in which he was merely a man.

On Elba, he recovered with characteristic speed. He reorganised the island's finances, built roads, improved the iron mines, and drilled his small garrison. He was a man who could not be idle. Within months, he was planning his return.

---

passages.section: 17. The Hundred Days — Return and Delusion (1815)
passages.text:
On 1 March 1815, Napoleon landed at Golfe-Juan near Antibes with 1,000 men. He marched north toward Paris, and the army sent to stop him defected to him instead. At Laffrey, near Grenoble, he faced a regiment of the Fifth Line and opened his coat to their muskets. "Soldiers, if there is one among you who would kill his Emperor, here I am." They rushed forward shouting "Vive l'Empereur!" It was the most audacious gamble of his life, and it worked because he understood something about loyalty and spectacle that no other leader of his era grasped — that men will follow a story they believe in, even against their orders.

Louis XVIII fled Paris. Napoleon entered the Tuileries on 20 March. He promised liberal reforms, a new constitution, peace with Europe. None of it was credible and much of it was sincere. He genuinely wanted to govern as a constitutional monarch. He genuinely believed the allies would accept his return. He was wrong on both counts, and his inability to see this — to recognise that the Europe of 1815 would not tolerate him regardless of what he promised — was the same cognitive failure that had sent him to Moscow. He predicted what he wanted rather than what was likely.

He was happy during the Hundred Days, or something close to it. He was back. He was Emperor. The adventure itself was the drug — the risk, the drama, the confirmation that he was the protagonist of history. But observers noted a new quality in him: a feverishness, a sense that he was running out of time, an awareness — suppressed but present — that this was the last act.

---

At Waterloo, Napoleon faced the Duke of Wellington's Anglo-allied army on a ridge near Brussels. His plan was sound: fix Wellington in place, then crush him with the Imperial Guard before Blücher's Prussians could arrive. But the execution was plagued by errors — not primarily his own but his subordinates'. Marshal Ney charged the British squares too early. Marshal Grouchy failed to prevent Blücher's approach. D'Erlon's corps attacked in a formation that maximised its vulnerability to British musketry.

Napoleon's reaction to these failures was fury. He raged at Ney. He cursed Grouchy. He blamed everyone except himself for the deteriorating situation. When the Old Guard finally advanced at 7:30 PM — the last reserve, the last hope — he watched from the rear, too exhausted and ill to lead the attack personally. The Guard advanced into devastating fire and broke. For the first time in its history, the Imperial Guard retreated. "La Garde recule!" The cry spread through the French army like a physical shock. If the Guard was beaten, everything was beaten.

The retreat became a rout. Napoleon was nearly captured. He fled to Paris, abdicated for the second time on 22 June, and surrendered to the British on 15 July, boarding HMS Bellerophon with a letter to the Prince Regent in which he compared himself to Themistocles — the Athenian general who had sought asylum from his former enemy. The comparison was grandiose, self-serving, and — in its way — not entirely wrong. He still believed he was the most important person in any room, any country, any century.

---

Napoleon arrived at St Helena in October 1815. The island was a volcanic rock in the South Atlantic, 1,200 miles from the nearest continent. His custodian was Sir Hudson Lowe, a meticulous, suspicious, and humourless man whom Napoleon despised and tormented in equal measure. They fought over everything — the size of the garden, the quality of the wine, the number of guards, whether Napoleon should be addressed as "Emperor" or "General Bonaparte." Lowe was following orders. Napoleon was fighting the only battles still available to him.

He dictated his memoirs — to Las Cases, Gourgaud, Montholon, Bertrand — and in doing so, he constructed the myth that would outlive the man. He rewrote his defeats as misfortunes, his mistakes as betrayals, his ambition as patriotism. The Egyptian campaign became a civilising mission. The Spanish war became a defensive necessity. The Russian campaign became a weather event. Waterloo was lost because of Grouchy, or Ney, or the rain, or fate — never because Napoleon had miscalculated.

This was not simply lying. It was something more psychologically complex: the construction of a narrative that allowed him to maintain his sense of self in conditions that should have destroyed it. If Napoleon admitted that Russia was a mistake, then everything that followed — Leipzig, abdication, Elba, Waterloo, St Helena — was a consequence of his own error. The weight of that admission would have been unbearable. So he built an alternative history in which he was always right and the universe was always unfair, and he believed it with the same intensity he had believed in his military plans. The self-deception was total and, in its way, heroic — a last campaign, fought against reality itself.

---

In his final years, Napoleon's health deteriorated. He suffered from chronic stomach pain — probably gastric cancer, the disease that had killed his father. He grew fat, lethargic, and withdrawn. The restless energy that had defined him was gone. He spent hours in the garden, tending plants. He read novels. He played cards. He quarrelled with his companions, who were themselves going mad from isolation and proximity.

He spoke often of his son, whom he had not seen since 1814. The boy was in Vienna, raised as an Austrian prince, taught to forget his father. Napoleon's grief over this separation was the most unguarded emotion of his exile. He did not rage or strategise or mythologise — he simply suffered. "I would have loved him," he said. "I would have made him a man." The conditional tense was the saddest thing about it: he was mourning not what he had lost but what he had never had.

He also reflected on what he had built and what it had cost. "I closed the gulf of anarchy and brought order out of chaos," he said. "I am the French Revolution." This was both grandiose and accurate. He had preserved the Revolution's legal and administrative achievements while extinguishing its democratic aspirations. Whether this was a rescue or a betrayal depended on whether you valued order or liberty — and Napoleon, to the end, valued order.

He reconciled with the Church, receiving last rites from a priest. His final words, on 5 May 1821, were disputed — some heard "France, armée, tête d'armée, Joséphine," others heard nothing coherent. He was fifty-one years old. He had been a king at thirty-five, master of Europe at thirty-six, and a prisoner at forty-six. His life was the most dramatic trajectory of rise and fall in modern history, and he had spent his last years making sure that the story of that trajectory would be told on his terms.

He succeeded. The myth he built at St Helena — of the martyred Emperor, the champion of the people, the man betrayed by lesser men — proved more durable than any of his military victories. It helped make his nephew Louis-Napoleon president and then emperor. It shaped French politics for a century. It continues to shape how we think about ambition, genius, and the cost of believing you are chosen by destiny. Napoleon's greatest victory was posthumous: he conquered not a country but a narrative.
